articles.title: Horror films exploit how human vision works to deliver movies’ best scares
articles.author: Arryn Robbins, Assistant Professor of Psychology, University of Richmond
paras: This article contains spoilers from popular horror movies and shows.

Imagine you’re in the movie theater watching 2018’s “Hereditary.” During one of the film’s most unsettling sequences, the main character, Peter, wakes up in bed disoriented. As he sits up, you hear a couple of gasps from others in the audience. The camera stays locked on Peter as he moves through his house and enters the dim living room.

You hear it again: more gasps. The lighting is low, a droning score builds tension, and your heart rate climbs. The people around you continue to audibly react. You haven’t seen anything scary yet, so what is everyone else responding to?
The camera slowly pulls back, and then you see her: Annie, Peter’s possessed mother, crouched on the ceiling in an unnatural way.
Watch the scene again and you might notice that Annie was in the shadows on the ceiling the whole time, following Peter through the house.
How could you have missed a human being on the ceiling, in plain view?

As a cognitive psychologist who studies visual perception, I’ve noticed that horror movies often exploit the gap between what’s in front of your eyes and what you consciously see. Directors and cinematographers act like folk cognitive psychologists, intuitively drawing your attention exactly where it needs to be to create a scare.
Horror movie fans have pointed out numerous examples of spooky figures and other unnoticed details in the background of scenes.

These blind spots exist because your visual system can’t process everything in a scene at once. You extract detailed information only from wherever your attention is directed. Anything outside the spotlight of your attention may go unnoticed, no matter how strange.

Inattentional blindness is the failure to notice something in plain view because your attention is engaged elsewhere; it’s the phenomenon behind the infamous invisible gorilla experiment, in which about half of participants busy counting basketball passes failed to notice a person in a gorilla suit strolling through the middle of the game.

Horror leans on inattentional blindness frequently, from the ghost boy in “Insidious” to the background ghosts scattered through Netflix’s “The Haunting of Hill House.” Something is plainly visible, though you often don’t notice it until a rewatch, and this delayed discovery can make the scene even creepier.

A related effect, change blindness, is the failure to notice something changing right in front of you. The difference can be as simple as a shirt color, or something drastic like the possessed girl Janet in “The Conjuring 2” morphing into an old man during her interview with Ed Warren. The camera stays on Ed while Janet sits slightly blurred in the background, making the transformation easy to miss until she abruptly changes back.
Directors also steer your attention to set up a scare, pulling your focus away from something creepy, or putting it in exactly the right spot just before a jump scare.

Eyeline match is a perfect example of this strategy. In “The Conjuring,” a girl sits up in bed, her fearful eyes fixed upward. The film cuts to reveal she’s staring at the ghost Bathsheba, crouched atop a wardrobe.

This editing technique works because it’s similar to something your visual system does: When someone near you looks sharply in one direction, your eyes follow automatically. Psychologists call this tendency gaze cueing, a reliable effect in attention research. Editing just mimics the real-life version to create tension, which resolves the moment you finally see what the character sees.

Sometimes directors do the opposite, giving your attention nothing to follow at all. The opening sequence of “It Follows” is a wide shot of a panicked girl running in and out of her house. With no eyeline or cut to guide you, the wide framing forces you into visual search, scanning corner to corner for a danger that may not even be there yet. Will something appear in a window? Follow her out the door? The uncertainty and the search build the tension.
The split between detecting and identifying

Your visual field isn’t equally good at everything: Some parts of your visual system perform the initial detection, others identify what was detected. For example, the fovea, a tiny pit in the retina that processes the spot you’re looking directly at, contains photoreceptors called cones that process fine detail and color.

Beyond that central spot is your peripheral vision, dominated by photoreceptors called rods that are sensitive to motion and low light rather than detail. In a sense, your peripheral vision is set up to help you quickly answer the question “Did something just move?”

When there’s motion at the edge of your vision, your peripheral system detects it almost instantly. Your eyes make a saccade – a rapid eye movement – to place the fovea onto the target to identify it. That gap between detecting and identifying can create a feeling of unease because something registered, something is there, but you can’t yet say what.

Playing with peripheral vision is almost a trope in horror movies now. Think of any hallway or mirror scene where you’re focused on a character and something moves behind them, grabbing your attention before you can figure out what it is.
Faces where there are none
Human beings evolved to quickly detect, identify and respond to potential threats, such as moving animals. That’s one reason vision is so sensitive to detecting movement.

It also explains why people are prone to pareidolia: the human bias toward detecting faces even where none exist. Have you ever seen a face in your curtains or toast? Missing a real face is potentially far costlier than perceiving a fake one, so our brains likely evolved to respond even to patterns that vaguely resemble faces.

“Midsommar” exploits pareidolia directly. As Dani is carried toward the feast after her crowning as May Queen, viewers have noticed a face in the trees. “The Night House” uses a similar trick, where ambiguous object configurations resolve into figures and faces that capture your attention. The 1963 film “The Haunting” does the same with a wall pattern during a particularly creepy scene.

Directors decide what you get to see and what they leave hidden, from ambiguous shapes to sudden movements to shadowy figures in the background. They seem to understand how your visual system works, and they use this knowledge to create tension in that space between perception and recognition, as your brain tries to determine what, exactly, you’re seeing.

articles.title: New long-clawed British dinosaur is the first of its kind in Europe
articles.author: Charlie Scherer, PhD Candidate in Earth Sciences, UCL
paras: The fossilised skull of a new species of mysterious meat-eating dinosaur from the Isle of Wight has been rediscovered in the collections of the Natural History Museum after over 100 years in storage.

Over its nearly 150-year history, this London museum has become home to over 30 million specimens, making it fairly easy to forget about the odd fossil or rock here and there. This is almost definitely what happened to the only known fossil of the UK’s newest dinosaur, a two-legged meat-eating theropod (the dinosaur family including birds) which we have named Invictibellatrix amberina in a new study.

In 2020, Paul Barrett, one of the museum’s palaeontologists, looked through the fossil collections and came across a small chunk of bone which he recognised as an important part of the skull of a dinosaur: the braincase. After going through museum records, he realised the braincase was found on a beach near Sudmoor Point of on the Isle of Wight, an island off the south coast of England known for its world-famous dinosaur fossils. Knowing that it came from the Isle of Wight, Barrett enlisted one of us (Cassius Morrison), a PhD student specialising in dinosaur braincases at the time, to study the fossil in detail and try to figure out which dinosaur it belonged to.
This work showed that the roughly 120 million year old fossil was unlike anything found from the island before and belonged to new species of a mysterious family of carnivores called the Megaraptora.

Megaraptorans are known for their slender skulls, lightly-built skeletons and gigantic hand claws, with some of the larger species having claws over 1 foot long. These ferocious predators are known from across the globe, with most species known from South America, particularly Argentina. Our new British species, Invictibellatrix amberina, was on the smaller side for megaraptorans, about 5 metres from head-to-tail and weighed as much a large tiger, making it the smallest known megaraptoran.

To study the new species, we compared it directly with the skulls of other carnivores. This involved playing a scientific version of spot-the-difference, looking at the subtle differences between species to work out what we were dealing with. We also used computed tomography (CT) scanning, which combines X-rays and computer processing to create detailed images, to look inside the braincase of Invictibellatrix and study what we could of its brain. Putting all of these findings into a computer algorithm to determine where our species sits in the family tree helped us to avoid bias in our interpretations.

Our work suggests that the new species was probably part of the early days of megaraptoran evolution, representing what these animals looked like before they grew to gigantic sizes, similar to their relatives the tyrannosaurs.

Invictibellatrix and its place in the theropod family tree are particularly important, as we now have a better understanding of when and how megaraptorans spread across the world. Before the discovery of Invictibellatrix, megaraptorans were only known from species of the early Cretaceous period (130-120 million years ago) of Thailand and Japan, plus multiple larger species from the late Cretaceous period (85–66 million years ago) of Australia and Argentina.

The great distances between these discoveries means that megaraptorans must have been even more common than their fossils suggest, since there is no way for large animals like these to swim across the oceans that separated these continents during the Cretaceous period.

As the first European megaraptoran, Invictibellatrix provides us with strong evidence that the group probably travelled to the southern continents from Asia, via Europe and Africa. Afterwards they probably spread out across South America and Australia sometime during, or perhaps even before, the early Cretaceous period. The fossil also implies that other megaraptorans may be waiting to be discovered in Africa and even Antarctica.

Invictibellatrix probably lived alongside other carnivores such as Neovenator (a relative of Allosaurus), Ceratosuchops (a relative of Spinosaurus) and Eotyrannus, which as the name implies, was an early relative to the Tyrannosaurus rex. These four dinosaurs were probably eating different animals to each other to survive. The spinosaur specialised in eating fish, with the others eating more land-based prey. Invictibellatrix probably fed on small dinosaurs, mammals, lizards and even crocodiles.

The story of megaraptorans seems to follow the pattern of most of nature’s successes. A small opportunist living in the shadows of much larger animals around the globe only to become the dominant force in a few select ecosystems up to the end of the age of dinosaurs.

It’s this story which gave Invictibellatrix amberina its name, honouring the role of megaraptorans as the apex predators in the late Cretaceous of South America. It translates to “unconquered [female] warrior of the amber”.

Invictibellatrix does not tell us everything. Scientists are still not sure when megaraptorans first evolved, but the fossil does give us some much-needed clues. There is so much left to be discovered about dinosaurs. Sometimes their secrets can be found simply hiding away in museum collections waiting for someone to come and take a closer look.

articles.title: What does a Starshield slowdown really mean for Ukraine’s war with Russia?
articles.author: Steve Uhlig, Professor of Networks and Head of School EECS, Queen Mary University of London
paras: Reports that SpaceX temporarily restricted its satellite internet service for Ukraine’s armed forces have generated serious concern in Kyiv and among the country’s allies. SpaceX operates the civilian Starlink system and its lesser-known military-grade counterpart, called Starshield.

But many news stories leave an important question unanswered: what does a Starshield “slowdown” mean on the battlefield? The answer is that it does not suddenly blind the Ukrainian military or bring operations to a halt. But it does degrade one of the communications systems deeply embedded in how Ukraine fights.

In modern warfare, connectivity is not simply a support function. It often controls drones, shares intelligence, updates targets, and keeps battlefield units coordinated. Ukraine has become particularly dependent on satellite communications since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Starlink and Starshield help to provide connectivity in situations where conventional telecommunications infrastructure has been damaged, destroyed or is subjected to electronic warfare.

According to Ukrainian officials and reporting citing US and Western sources, terminals operating under the Starshield service were restricted when mounted on platforms moving faster than about 100 mph (161 km/h). The change reportedly disrupted drone operations and other military activities that rely on high-speed mobile connectivity.

To understand why that matters, consider how Ukraine uses satellite connectivity in practice. Frontline units frequently depend on satellite links to transmit video, receive intelligence and maintain communications over long distances.

Commanders commonly rely on near real-time battlefield information to coordinate operations across dispersed units. When that information flow slows, becomes intermittent, or stops altogether – as with the “speed limit” imposed on platforms moving quicker than 100 mph – the effects can quickly spread beyond the individual operator who loses connectivity.

The most immediate impact is likely to be on drones. Many Ukrainian systems lean on satellite connectivity not because drones cannot physically fly without it, but because modern operations often require continuous communication between operators and aircraft.

A reconnaissance drone may stream live video back to command centres. An interceptor drone pursuing an incoming Russian target may require rapid updates and coordination. A strike mission may depend on real-time intelligence and target confirmation.

When connectivity becomes intermittent or unavailable, the missions slow down, become less accurate, and, in some cases, become impossible. Military personnel cited in media reports described missions being cancelled and connections dropping out during operations.

Even brief interruptions can matter. A drone travelling at high speed can cover a significant distance in ten or 20 seconds. During a critical manoeuvre or interception, losing communications for that long may mean losing the target or the aircraft altogether.

The restrictions may be particularly significant because Ukraine increasingly uses drones not only for long-range strikes but also for air defence. Ukrainian officials have stated that satellite-connected interceptor drones are among the tools used against Russian attack drones. Any reduction in connectivity therefore potentially affects not only offensive operations as well as the protection of cities and critical infrastructure.

A common misconception is that satellite internet is simply another communications channel that can readily be replaced. In practice, alternatives exist, but none offers the same combination of coverage, mobility and resilience.
Conventional military radios stay essential, but their range is limited. Fibre-optic networks provide excellent performance, but only where infrastructure exists and remains intact.

Microwave links require suitable terrain and installations. All can be vulnerable to disruption in wartime conditions. Satellite systems are attractive precisely because they can continue operating when much of the terrestrial communications infrastructure is under pressure.

This raises another question: if SpaceX owns the technology, how can the White House influence its use? That issue remains somewhat opaque. Reuters reported, citing US and Western officials, that the White House instructed SpaceX to slow Starshield service and passed the order through the Pentagon. The officials did not identify who made the decision. A senior US official reportedly denied that the US president Donald Trump himself ordered it directly.

Part of the explanation lies in the distinction between Starlink and Starshield. Starlink is SpaceX’s commercial broadband service. By contrast, Starshield was developed specifically for government and national security customers and operates under US government contracts.
Elon Musk has publicly argued that Starshield systems are “owned and controlled” by the US government and that limits on their use are determined by the US military and, ultimately, the president.

The precise contractual and operational arrangements are not public, and some analysts dispute the idea that SpaceX has no operational role whatsoever. Nevertheless, Starshield is fundamentally different from a consumer internet service.

When governments procure military communications systems, they generally acquire varying degrees of authority over how those systems are used. The relationship is best understood, not as the White House ordering a private technology company around, but as a government customer exercising influence over a capability integrated into national security operations.
An alternative to Starshield?

The episode also raises the question of whether Ukraine could switch to an alternative provider. The answer is: partially, but not quickly. The most frequently cited alternative is Eutelsat’s OneWeb network. This European-owned low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation already provides services in Ukraine and has previously indicated a willingness to expand its support.

However, OneWeb operates a substantially smaller constellation than Starlink and was designed primarily for enterprise and institutional connectivity rather than the mass deployment of tens of thousands of highly portable user terminals.

As a result, while OneWeb could supplement existing communications and reduce dependence on a single provider. Defence analysts generally regard it as an enhancement rather than a complete replacement for the Starlink ecosystem. Replacing Starlink is not simply a question of launching more satellites.
It would require new terminals, new contracts, new operational procedures and extensive integration with systems that have evolved around Starlink technology over several years of war.

Strikes can damage terrestrial networks, radios have range and bandwidth limits, and fixed infrastructure is vulnerable to attack. Starlink became so critical to Ukraine because it combines mobility, high bandwidth, and resilience at a scale few direct competitors can match.

The wider lesson may be strategic rather than technical. Ukraine’s military has benefited enormously from satellite connectivity, but the debate reveals the risks of dependence on a single provider, however capable.

The episode demonstrates that communications networks can become instruments of policy as well as technology. On today’s battlefield, controlling the flow of data can be almost as consequential as controlling the movement of troops.

For Ukraine, the Starshield slowdown matters not because of the loss of a single communications system, but because it reminds us that access to critical digital infrastructure can be as important, and as vulnerable, as access to weapons.

articles.title: Why haven’t farm animals evolved against humans? A biologist explains why there won’t be a chicken uprising anytime soon
articles.author: Alida de Flamingh, Assistant Professor of Evolutionary Genomics, University of Tennessee
paras: Curious Kids is a series for children of all ages. If you have a question you’d like an expert to answer, send it to CuriousKidsUS@theconversation.com.
Why haven’t farm animals evolved to protect themselves against humans? – Sarang, age 15, Latur, Maharashtra, India
Have you ever wondered why dogs get the zoomies or wag their tails? One answer comes from a rather unexpected source: foxes.

A team of scientists bred captured silver foxes for tameness, choosing the least fearful and aggressive animals to become parents. They repeated this process with each litter of pups, avoiding any training and limiting their exposure to people.
Within six generations, the foxes began to show some familiar, doglike behaviors. Some wagged their tails as people approached, licked their hands and even liked to be petted.
These silver foxes are a remarkable example of selective breeding, where people choose animals with particular traits to produce the next generation of animals.

Selective breeding is the driving force behind domestication: the process through which animal populations adapted to life alongside people over many generations. Dogs are considered the first animals that humans domesticated, originally descending from wolves.
Domestication and evolution

Another team of scientists studied the genes of ancient animals to understand how domestication has shaped farm animals over time. They examined the genetics of a wide range of traits, from coat color in goats and horses to aggression and egg production in chickens.

Farmers might selectively breed chickens for more eggs, or cows for more milk. They may also favor calmer animals because they are easier to handle. Because animals with these traits are chosen more frequently by farmers for breeding, their genes have a better chance of reaching the next generation.
This process is domestication in action: Inherited traits such as tameness, producing more food or having a coat color preferred by people become common over generations.

Farm animals that are aggressive or don’t produce much food may be less useful to humans, thereby “protecting” themselves from being used by people. But with people in charge, these animals will also likely be excluded from breeding and have less of a chance of passing their genes on.
On the farm, people hold all the power. Because of the process of domestication through selective breeding, farm animals cannot evolve to protect themselves from humans.
Human influence in the wild
People can influence evolution in the wild even without deciding which animals to breed.

Animals with traits that help them evade humans who are trying to hunt or capture them will tend to pass on their genes to the next generation. This means that, in the wild, animal populations may evolve more protective characteristics, since people aren’t directly involved in selecting which animals will breed and pass on their genes.

Consider the elephants of Gorongosa National Park in Mozambique, a species I study in my work as an evolutionary biologist. During the country’s civil war, poachers hunted large numbers of elephants for their ivory tusks.

Some females were naturally tuskless, making them less likely to be targeted. As a result, these tuskless females had a better chance of surviving, reproducing and passing on the genes associated with tusklessness. Over generations, tusklessness became more common in the population.
While these elephants did not deliberately evolve a defense against hunters, tusklessness provided a survival benefit. Therefore, evolution favored an existing trait that offered some protection.

From friendly foxes to tuskless elephants, human choices can shape how animal populations evolve. Sometimes people do this deliberately, by breeding animals for desired traits. Other times, human impact on the environment alone can change which animals survive and reproduce, and therefore shape how species evolve.
Next time your dog snuggles up, remember those foxes!

And since curiosity has no age limit – adults, let us know what you’re wondering, too. We won’t be able to answer every question, but we will do our best.

articles.title: NASA’s Mars orbiter fleet is getting old – here’s how that could affect future exploration
articles.author: Margaret Landis, Assistant Professor of Earth and Space Exploration, Arizona State University
paras: Currently, about 16,000 satellites are orbiting Earth, providing everything from GPS service and weather reports to phone service in remote locations to people across the globe.
In contrast, the highest-ever number of active satellites in orbit around Mars, one of the best-explored other planets in our solar system, is eight.

Starting in 2021, there were three from NASA, two from the European Space Agency and one each from the Indian Space Research Organization, the UAE Space Agency and the China National Space Administration. The oldest of these is still 2001 Mars Odyssey, which has now spent 25 years in space, with Mars Express, at 23 years, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, at 20 years, hot on its heels.
But in December 2025, NASA lost contact with its Maven spacecraft, bringing the total number of active satellites down to seven, and NASA’s to two.
The cause of the loss of Maven has still not been publicly released, and NASA officially declared the mission over in June 2026. A final report on the cause of the loss is due later this year.

NASA is exploring potential commercial solutions to supplement the current fleet of Mars orbiters. In September 2026, NASA selected Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin to provide a Mars telecommunication satellite no later than Dec. 31, 2028.

These satellites are important because future missions will rely on them to communicate with Earth and select safe landing sites on Mars. Planetary scientists like me rely on the data they’ve taken over the past few decades to learn more about our close, red neighbor.
Maven loss and implications

The Mars Atmosphere and Volatile EvolutioN, or Maven, spacecraft arrived at Mars in 2014, making it NASA’s youngest orbiter. It was only briefly the youngest in the international Mars family, as the Indian space agency’s Mars Orbiting Mission spacecraft arrived a few days later.

The longer any satellite spends in space, the greater the toll of the harsh environment – from extreme temperature swings to solar radiation. Maven, however, appeared generally healthy until it missed a radio check-in – a sign of trouble – after emerging back from behind the planet.

Whatever happened to Maven last December was only the second time in the 21st century that NASA had lost contact with an orbiter during otherwise ordinary operations. The other time was in 2006, with Mars Global Surveyor, which NASA ultimately lost, likely due to issues with uploaded software commands.

The Mars exploration community, myself among them, is waiting with bated breath to understand why one-third of NASA’s Mars fleet lost contact seemingly overnight. The loss ends a stellar, almost two-decade-long track record of missions ending when expected, not before.

Mars science has been in a golden age since 2001 Mars Odyssey arrived at the red planet 25 years ago. NASA has had a Mars rover of some type operating on the surface continuously since 2004 with the Exploration rover landings, so there have been only a handful of years in the 21st century where scientists couldn’t access nearly simultaneous views of Mars from the surface and from orbit.

This access gives Mars scientists the ability to study how both the surface and atmosphere change over time. In particular, we can follow changes with Mars’ seasons, which drive about a quarter of its atmosphere onto its surface as seasonal ice. And we have found laundry lists of these changing features, including “spiderlike” araneiform features in the soil that likely develop from carbon dioxide geysers.

Learning about rare events like global dust storms, which obscure Mars’ entire surface, also opens up many new questions. We still don’t know what triggers the start of a global dust storm, and they only occur every several Mars years. In Maven’s 11 years at Mars, it was only able to observe one global dust storm, in 2018.

From a practical standpoint, Mars orbiters have their own science missions. However, their powerful radios are also critical for delivering data from landers and rovers, like Perseverance or Curiosity, back to Earth. In the past, NASA has adjusted the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter and Maven orbits to support landings and surface operations.

HiRISE (High-Resolution Imaging Science Experiment) aboard the Reconnaissance orbiter, is the highest-resolution camera in orbit to date. Engineers have used data from HiRISE to ensure they could deliver the Mars rovers Curiosity and Perseverance to the surface, as well as the InSight lander.

While Mars orbiters and their instrument suites are selected for their science value, they have come to participate in infrastructure that is essential for getting all the possible data back to Earth. These tasks, which go beyond science data collection, make the orbiter fleet critical to Mars exploration.

The Dec. 31, 2028, delivery date for the Blue Origin telecommunications Mars orbiter to NASA represents the earliest a new orbiter could be launched for Mars. Mars launch opportunities happen at an approximately 2-year cadence, when Mars and Earth get closest to each other in their respective orbits. During this window, less fuel is needed for the journey.

If a new Mars orbiter for science or telecommunications is not launched by the 2028 window, the next opportunity would be in 2030 or 2031. While the Blue Origin telecommunications orbiter would support future exploration missions, the announcement did not outline plans for any science instrumentation onboard.

Mars Odyssey will be around 30 years old by then, and the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter around 25. NASA hardware tends to be hardy, often greatly exceeding expectations. For example, the Mars Exploration rovers were meant to last for 90 days, with Spirit ending its mission after over six years and Opportunity after over 14 years. However, orbiters may slowly lose capability over time – the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter’s spectrometer instrument ceased operations in 2023, while its other instruments are still active.
But three or four decades in a space environment is a long tour of duty for any hardware in space, let alone hardware that is pulling double-duty as scientist and radio broadcaster.

Much like driving your first car for far longer than you had planned on, the NASA orbiter fleet is waiting to see if the next repair bill means it’s time for an upgrade, or if it’ll have to catch rides from its friends.

Until NASA releases its report, scientists and engineers will be waiting to understand what happened to end the Maven spacecraft’s mission early, and how those details can help them keep the current fleet flying until reinforcements finally arrive.

Margaret Landis receives funding from NASA, including as a Co-Investigator on the HiRISE Mars camera instrument. She is a long-term member of the Planetary Society, and formerly worked at the University of Colorado, Boulder, the lead organization for the MAVEN mission.

articles.title: Why calling for a ‘kill switch’ is the wrong way to think about reining in AI
articles.author: Trent Wintermeier, Ph.D. Candidate in Rhetoric and Writing, The University of Texas at Austin
paras: In the wake of high-profile hacking incidents involving advanced artificial intelligence agents, some politicians and business executives have been calling for an AI kill switch: a safeguard that could shut down these AI systems in an emergency.
The idea is that, if a model were to behave in dangerous ways, a kill switch would allow humans to regain control over that system by metaphorically flipping a switch from “on” to “off.”

Several efforts at AI regulation in 2026 have focused on the notion of a kill switch. These include proposed congressional legislation such as the AI Kill Switch Act, and California Gov. Gavin Newsom’s executive order aimed at reining in AI. President Donald Trump has opposed the idea of an AI kill switch as unnecessary regulation, and to date there has been no national regulation that includes a kill switch.

Experts such as Dylan Baker, a research engineer at the nonprofit Distributed AI Research Institute, have explained that one regulatory problem with the metaphor of the kill switch is that today’s advanced AI models involve a complex infrastructure of distributed technologies, which is beyond the control of a single kill switch.

Additionally, the metaphor of the kill switch also obscures the human decisions involved in the responsibility and oversight of an out-of-control model. The problem is that the metaphor does not account for the technological or human aspects of AI.
Black boxes and kill switches

The metaphor of the kill switch is not necessarily new. In fact, it is rooted in the same rhetoric as the black box metaphor, which similarly blurs the complex aspects of AI by framing inner workings as confined and unintelligible. Referring to AI as a black box frames these systems in terms of restricted incomprehensibility: a monolithic stranger to human control and understanding.

As the University of Cambridge, digital humanities researcher Eryk Salvaggio argues that “the black box of AI cultivates useful confusion about what can and cannot be known” about the complexity of frontier models. The idea of the kill switch cultivates a similar confusion by obscuring the distributed infrastructure and human influence that are important aspects of AI. While these metaphors have opposite meanings – resisting control and regaining control – they invoke the same implicit argument about the nuts and bolts of AI.

Both the black box and kill switch are what cognitive linguist George Lakoff and philosopher Mark Johnson call structural metaphors. They rely on simple physical concepts – for example, object, substance, up-down and in-out. Structural metaphors use one clearly delineated concept to help make another concept clearer. For example, black box uses the concept of an opaque container to give a clear structure to the concept of hidden or inscrutable inner workings.

Additionally, Lakoff and Johnson say that this type of metaphor can also hide some aspects of a concept by focusing attention on others. For example, the kill switch metaphor hides the complexity of advanced AI models by focusing on the fact that a model can be on or off.

What this means is that framing the operation of AI in terms of a black box and kill switch relies on the straightforward ideas of “box” and “switch” to conceal the complex operations of AI. Reining in AI becomes difficult on a policy level when discussions about AI regulation fail to account for the infrastructural and human aspects of advanced models.
Centralization and ‘rogue’ AI

There are two problems with the structural metaphor of an AI kill switch, both demonstrating that it misses the mark for a national safeguard. The first is that a kill switch makes the global infrastructure supporting AI appear centralized, when in reality it is a web of interconnected technologies spread across the globe.

The advanced models that companies like OpenAI and Anthropic are concerned about releasing rely on multiple computers and data centers that are spread out nationally. It is not as simple as pulling a plug, opening a box or flipping a switch. The kill switch metaphor reduces the infrastructural entanglements of AI to outdated ideas about technology. For instance, in proposing his since-failed “AI Emergency Button Act” bill, Sen. John Kennedy compared the concept to kill switches in machines such as jet skis.

The second problem is that the kill switch idea keeps hidden the human decision-making involved in the training and deployment of frontier models. Rather than serving as a reminder that people are involved, the kill switch positions the human outside of the loop and ready to flip the switch during a catastrophic emergency. Human intervention is invoked as an afterthought, instead of a process that involves training, supervision and approval.

For instance, accounts of how OpenAI’s model went “rogue” and hacked AI company Hugging Face depict the AI agents as though they operated on their own agenda. But experts have explained that not only did OpenAI personnel turn off safety mechanisms, but they also gave the model impossible tasks and left a door open to the internet. The role people played counters the “rogue” agent framing.

The kill switch metaphor is ill-suited to the challenge of regulating AI because there is no way to switch off an AI model without accounting for its distributed infrastructure and human influence. There is no big red button, emergency brake or glass box hiding a lever. Effective national regulation of AI will not begin with any single switch or any one person’s finger.

articles.title: Digital natives are buying electric cars as if they were smartphones
articles.author: Svetoslav Georgiev, Associate Professor, School of Intelligent Finance and Business, Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University
paras: Until recently, buying a car meant obsessing over horsepower, transmission types and brand heritage. But step into the market today and the showroom floor looks entirely different.
With the aggressive expansion of electric vehicle production and the entry of smartphone giants like Xiaomi and Huawei into the car market, vehicles are rapidly transforming into rolling computers.
This shift raises a fundamental question for the modern market: are younger consumers beginning to evaluate cars the exact same way they evaluate smartphones?

To understand the buying behaviour of young consumers, we must first recognise that the car industry is undergoing a profound digital transformation. Traditional factors like brand prestige and mechanical engineering, while still relevant, are steadily losing ground to software capabilities and digital integration.

Tech-focused manufacturers are prioritising software-driven car systems, leaving legacy car makers struggling to adapt. For millenials, this technological pivot is not just an added bonus; it is becoming a baseline expectation.

Market-specific factors like electric vehicle pricing and availability in regions like China may accelerate this trend, but the underlying data reflects a broader, cross-national generational shift among digital natives (someone who grew up around digital technology, such as smartphones) are revealing this shift in China, North America and Europe.
A generational perspective
When technologically minded consumers encounter an electric vehicle, they do not necessarily see a mechanical machine with a motor; they see a hardware platform waiting for an operating system.

Consequently, this mindset shifts how they judge the vehicle’s core anatomy. When this demographic evaluates electric vehicles, they base their decisions heavily on “product technological development” (how well the in-car technology works, for instance) and “charging infrastructure” alongside financial incentives.
This directly mirrors how a consumer evaluates a smartphone’s operational speed, battery longevity, and software updates rather than traditional, outdated car metrics.

This paradigm shift also rewrites how cars are bought and experienced. Long before a consumer ever sits in a driver’s seat, the purchasing journey has fundamentally changed. Younger consumers demonstrate a strong inclination toward online platforms and social media as their primary shopping channels, relying heavily on digital interactions and visually rich experiences.

Rather than turning to traditional dealership visits or print brochures, they depend on user-generated content, peer opinions, online reviews and digital advertising to inform their purchasing decisions. Furthermore, recent studies show that this target group’s evaluation criteria continue to mirror the metrics they apply to mobile technology.

When car shopping, research shows that gen Z consumers seek out technologically advanced and highly personalised experiences, showing a specific interest in the entertainment capabilities and software ecosystems of modern vehicles. This indicates they are evaluating the digital and entertainment experience inside the car, much like they would evaluate the apps of a new phone.

The intense brand loyalty traditionally reserved for Apple or android phones has seamlessly transferred to the car market. Seamless ecosystem integration via systems like Apple CarPlay or Android Auto is treated as a mandatory requirement. If a car fails to mirror a driver’s digital life instantly, it fails the test.

Younger consumers scrutinise a vehicle’s multimedia and infotainment systems with the same hardware expectations they apply to smartphones. If a touchscreen exhibits input lag, clunky user interfaces, or poor user experiences, it severely damages their perception of the entire vehicle.

Unlike older generations who harbour a habitual attachment to driving, younger cohorts base their transport choices on metrics such as travel time, cost efficiency and service reliability. They evaluate transport options rationally rather than emotionally.

Younger demographics increasingly prioritise shared mobility programmes, such as Uber and Grab, over private vehicle ownership. They expect personal settings and digital profiles to sync instantly upon entering any vehicle. This allows them to listen to their latest music playlists or read messages on their smartphone. This mirrors the multi-device continuity they experience when using, for example, tablets and smartphones.

Just as smartphone consumers agonise over app permissions and data tracking, tech-savvy millennials, as well as gen Zs, view connected cars through a lens of data security. Trust in the way vehicle technology and data is handled have become a primary psychological barrier to adoption.

However, a fundamental disconnect explains a striking corporate blind spot identified in recent market research: while 80% of automotive executives believe they are delivering an exceptional digital customer experience, only 8% of customers actually agree. Traditional manufacturers are failing the software test because they still think like mechanics, not app developers.

Treating a car like a smartphone, however, raises a potential problem related to the physical reality of driving. While younger consumers demand the deep customisation and flexibility of touchscreens, replacing physical controls with digital sub-menus creates massive cognitive overload.

Forcing drivers to navigate complex digital layers to adjust basic climate or safety settings diverts visual attention and increases the risks of an accident. One study argues that reaction times using screens while driving are worse than being drunk or under the influence of drugs.

This has sparked an inevitable regulatory and design backlash. Safety organisations and designers are pushing back against pure “touchscreen-isation”, noting that a car is ultimately a high-speed vehicle, not a handset.

Even major car manufacturers, such as Volkswagen and Mazda, have publicly admitted that eliminating physical buttons was a misstep, leading to a hybrid design mandate where tactile controls for core functions must coexist with digital entertainment.
Ultimately, younger consumers are evaluating cars through a smartphone-tinted lens. Yet, the future of the car market will not belong to the brands that simply build iPhones on wheels.
The winners will be the manufacturers that successfully balance the digital native’s craving for software-driven connectivity with the uncompromising, safety-first reality of car design.

articles.title: The 17th-century British scientists who investigated hauntings
articles.author: Louise Ryland-Epton, Visiting Fellow in History, The Open University
paras: About 1671, parson Symonds, who officiated at Garsdon church in north Wiltshire in south west England, was riding home late one night when a spectre leapt up behind him. The spectre rode parallel to him until they came to the parsonage, where it jumped off. The apparition then turned to face Symonds, and “gap’d at him”. Symonds identified the ghost as that of John Estcourt, a gentleman who had died about two years earlier.

Halloween is all about witches and ghosts. In English scientific circles in the second half of the 17th century, there was a discussion about whether such things existed and how their existence could be proved.

The Royal Society, founded in 1660, was the country’s principal scientific institution. Joseph Glanvill, a Royal Society fellow, investigated spirits and witches. His Saducismus Triumphatus (1681) aimed to prove their existence by cataloguing cases in detail. He argued that denying them was to deny God’s existence.

Symonds’ haunting was recorded by that of another of the society’s fellows, John Aubrey, in a survey of Wiltshire’s natural world. Aubrey agreed with Glanvill that the supernatural deserved serious study and directed his readers to Saducismus, but he thought Glanvill somewhat gullible.
Aubrey was born in 1626 at Easton Piercy, a few miles from Garsdon. I have edited John Aubrey’s Natural History to mark his 400th anniversary.

This natural history of Wiltshire was begun in 1656 and was the first English county survey of nature to be attempted – although by the time he finished it, decades later, other surveys had already been published. It was an important scientific work, and in 1691, acknowledging that, the Royal Society had the Natural History copied and added to its library.

Its subject matter is highly idiosyncratic, and Aubrey sometimes goes off on tangents. He covers swan-sized dragons in north Africa in a chapter on birds and the existence of giants in a section called “Men and Women”. Almost at the end of the text is a chapter titled “Accidents” that records extraordinary events, including supernatural ones, like the haunting of Symonds.
Aubrey has long been seen as naive, partly because of Miscellanies (1696), the only book he published, which recorded tales of the unexplained. In the Natural History, he was clear:

Though I myselfe never saw any such things, yet I will not conclude that there is no truth at all in these reports. I believe that extraordinarily there have been such apparitions: but where one is true, a hundred are figments.

He also documented exposed frauds, such as Katherine Waldron, who pretended to be bewitched and endured pins being driven into her flesh to prove it. As the objective of natural history at this time was to gather evidence from which new scientific theories could be developed, Aubrey’s method in chronicling cases was entirely in keeping with the aims of scientific enterprise.

So, Aubrey was neither uncritical nor dismissive about Symonds’ story. Symonds was “a lusty strong fellow”, presumably not someone nervous or hysterical and prone to flights of imagination. His position as a churchman also gave authority to his testimony. Yet Aubrey noted a French saying that drunk men saw devils, a sceptical observation that cast doubt on the account. But he concluded with a strange detail: it was corroborated by the parson’s horse, “that trembled and sweat, when he came home and continued to do so the next day, and would not eat his oates”. The horse could not lie or get drunk; its fear, manifest in the trembling and sweat, was genuine.

Aubrey recorded another anecdote about a night ride. It concerned Sir Ralph Bankes’ valet:“a briske young fellow”, who, riding late over Badbury Warren, Dorset, discerned something that looked black, which, as he approached, became bigger.
Feare came upon him, and he protested his haire stood on end: but thought he, I have but a life to lose and I will see it, be it spirit or not.
The valet spurred his horse and came to the place, only to find the apparition was “a heap of horse dung”.

In Symonds’ haunting, the truth of the spectre could not be tested; but witnesses were recorded, and their testimony weighed. In the valet’s case, the witness tested the truth of the ghost himself and found it was a pile of dung.

Aubrey applied the same empirical method throughout his Natural History to both natural and supernatural phenomena. He assembled evidence with care, tested it if he could and resisted easy conclusions. It’s an approach worth remembering this Halloween when fantastical tales hit your social media feed. A phantom may prove to be a load of poo.

Louise Ryland-Epton's work on John Aubrey was supported at an early stage by a David Walker Memorial Visiting Fellowship in Early Modern History at the Bodleian Library, University of Oxford.This article draws on ghost stories recorded in John Aubrey’s Natural History, which she edited for Hobnob Press.

articles.title: Scientists are growing human brain tissue in living mice – could this make their welfare harder to assess?
articles.author: Mackenzie Graham, Senior Research Fellow, University of Oxford
paras: What happens when scientists start changing the brain – the very system through which an animal’s mental states are expressed in behaviour?

In a recent study published in Nature, researchers implanted human brain organoids – small, simplified structures grown from human stem cells – into the brains of living mice. Over time, these organoids developed and integrated with the mouse nervous system.

Transplanting organoids composed of human cells into animals, including their brains, is not new. However, previous experiments faced an obstacle: human brain cells grow much more slowly than mouse brain cells, and so organoids are quickly “out-competed” before they can fully integrate with the mouse brain. In the new study, scientists genetically altered mice so that parts of their brain did not develop, then transplanted the human organoids into the vacant space.

The idea of creating human-animal chimeras – animals containing human cells – raises ethical questions, particularly when involving the brain. Various philosophers have argued that as the proportion of human brain tissue increases, we should consider whether the animal could acquire human-like mental capacities – and whether this should change how we treat it. But I argue that serious questions about our ability to recognise animal suffering will arise long before mice gain increased intelligence.
What is it like to be a mouse?

The philosopher Thomas Nagel asked a version of this question about bats. He argued that conscious beings have a specific experience of the world, but that others cannot access that experience from the outside. Instead, we must infer what others experience. With animals, we do this through their behaviour and physiology. But this approach assumes that we understand how what we observe relates to what the animal experiences.

There is nothing morally important about a cell simply because it came from a human. Imagine two mice with identical mental lives and cognitive abilities, one produced using transplanted human cells and the other through a modification involving only mouse cells. It is difficult to see why the first should matter more simply because some of its cells are human.
If chimeras pose a moral problem, it is more plausibly because of changes to their cognitive capacities, than because they blur a species boundary.

There are good reasons to doubt that a mouse containing human brain cells could develop anything resembling human intelligence. This is because human-like cognition does not emerge simply from having enough human neural cells. A mouse containing human cortical neurons still has mouse sensory systems, a mouse body and develops according to species specific processes. All of these factors impose constraints on the kinds of cognitive capacities it might acquire.

Animal welfare science depends on interpretation. A mouse cannot report that it is stressed or in pain, so researchers rely on behavioural and physiological indicators. Changes in nesting, social interaction or facial expressions associated with pain, for example, can provide evidence about mouse welfare.

Changing an animal’s brain complicates these interpretations. This is because it alters the very biological system responsible for generating an animal’s experiences, and for producing much of the behaviour through which we infer those experiences.
A mouse might still seem to behave “like a mouse” even as we become less certain that its behaviour accurately tells us how it feels.

In the recent Nature study, researchers reported that mice which received the organoid implant performed on a par with healthy control mice on short-term memory tasks (such as navigating a maze). The researchers did not observe any evidence of altered behaviour or increased intelligence.

This is reassuring. But suppose a chimera grooms less than an ordinary mouse. Researchers can still measure that difference accurately, but interpreting it as evidence of distress means we’re assuming that grooming retains roughly the same relationship to the animal’s experiences as it does in an ordinary mouse.

The same applies to the observation of “normal” mouse behaviour. Since we don’t know exactly how changing the brain will change behaviour, this could make it harder to recognise if the indicators of poor welfare we rely upon are no longer accurate.
What follows for research?

Organoids grown in a dish have been important tools for studying human brain development and disease. But a dish cannot reproduce the environment of a living brain. Transplantation allows researchers to study human brain cells as they develop within a functioning nervous system, potentially providing better models of brain disorders and new ways to test treatments.

This does not, by itself, settle the debate over whether research using chimeras should stop. Uncertainty about an animal’s welfare does not automatically mean that its welfare is worse. It could, in principle, be better. Abandoning potentially valuable research also carries a cost.

Proposals researchers have made for overseeing studies involving chimeras already emphasise careful behavioural monitoring. But this may not be enough. Researchers may also need to establish that the indicators they measure continue to tell us what we think they do. As neural interventions become more extensive, researchers may therefore need to re-validate their methods of welfare assessment.

What happens if we eventually create an animal with human-like intelligence or consciousness? We may never reach that point. But we do not need to reach it before chimeras present a difficult ethical problem. Long before we create an animal that thinks like us, we may create one whose behaviour we no longer understand.
Mackenzie Graham receives funding from The Kavli Foundation, and the National Institute for Health Research.

articles.title: For centuries, bird migration was a mystery – a tech revolution is changing that, and could help save these amazing creatures
articles.author: Peter P. Marra, Dean of The Earth Commons, Professor of Biology and the Environment, Georgetown University
paras: For more than 2,000 years, scientists have scratched their heads over one of the most basic mysteries of the natural world: Where do birds go?

Billions of birds appear and disappear with the seasons every year. Early naturalists offered explanations for the disappearances that today seem fantastical: Birds transformed into other species, one theory went. Others suggested they hibernated underwater or even migrated to the moon.
The truth, that these small animals were traveling thousands of miles across the planet, must once have seemed just as improbable.

Then, in the early 1800s, dramatic evidence emerged supporting the theory of migration. White storks began appearing in Germany with African arrows embedded in their bodies. These birds became known as pfeilstörche, or “arrow storks.” They provided compelling evidence that birds disappearing from Europe were traveling all the way to Africa and back.
Almost two centuries later, scientists are still asking the same question, but our ability to answer it has been transformed.

For most of ornithological history, scientists understood migration through brief glimpses of a bird, a specimen collected somewhere else, or the rare instance of a banded bird recovered hundreds or thousands of miles from where it had been marked. From these fragments of intelligence, scientists reconstructed journeys that took place largely beyond their view.
Today, it’s possible to see the journeys themselves, almost in real time.
A century of following birds

Bird banding was the first tool used to attempt a systematic approach to connect these fragments of information. Since the early 1900s, researchers have placed uniquely numbered metal bands on birds and hoped someone, somewhere, would encounter them again.

Of more than 79 million birds banded, only about 6.5 million have been recovered. That generally told scientists just two things: where a bird was banded and where it was encountered again. Everything between them remained invisible.
Over the past quarter-century or so, the tools used to determine where birds go have changed dramatically.

Tracking devices can now be carried by increasingly smaller birds, recording their movements and communicating with land-based receivers or satellites orbiting the earth. Testing stable isotopes in feathers and other tissues can reveal where a bird originated. Genetic testing can distinguish populations.
At the same time, the extraordinary growth of bird-watching and citizen science has created another revolution.

Millions of observations by bird-watchers submitted to eBird, an online database to record the birds they see, show the distribution and abundance of birds across a continent throughout the year in ways early ornithologists could scarcely have imagined.
Collectively, these methods open an extraordinary new window into migratory birds and one of nature’s most remarkable behaviors: migration.
Discovering unknown migrations
More than 70% of North American bird species are migratory. Yet scientists have known surprisingly little about where specific populations go.

A species like the American robin may breed across thousands of miles of North America, with different breeding populations migrating to entirely different places for the winter. Birds breeding in one part of the continent may travel one route and encounter one set of environmental conditions, while members of the same species experience a completely different set of conditions along another route.

These connections between where a bird breeds and where it spends the winter is called migratory connectivity. They are critical for understanding everything from the consequences of climate change on birds to how avian pathogens and diseases spread, to a species’ basic ecology.

We are ornithologists and conservation scientists who have spent almost 15 years along with a team of contributors compiling this rapidly expanding knowledge on bird movement into The Atlas of North America’s Migratory Birds. It is being published Nov. 3, 2026, by Princeton University Press, with all profits going to bird conservation and research in Latin America and the Caribbean. The atlas covers the latest information on seasonal movements for nearly 600 species and combines a century of bird-banding data with eBird observations, tracking studies, stable isotope testing, genetics and other sources of information.
What emerges is a picture of migratory birds that is both more complicated and more remarkable than the simple arrows pointing between breeding and wintering ranges on a map.

Consider the yellow-billed cuckoo. These birds breed over a wide range of the eastern two-thirds of the U.S. but migrate to a relatively small wintering area in the Gran Chaco region of northern Argentina, Paraguay and southern Bolivia.
In contrast, peregrine falcons that breed in Alaska migrate almost directly south, dispersing across the Americas to wintering grounds that extend as far as southern South America.
Discoveries like these are accumulating rapidly. Collectively, they amount to a renaissance in our understanding of animal movement never before imagined.
The more clearly scientists can follow individual birds and populations across the planet, the more extraordinary these species can seem.

Migratory birds such as the arctic tern and northern wheatear cross oceans, deserts and mountain ranges. Some, like the bar-tailed godwits, fly thousands of miles without stopping. Others, like the American redstart, return year after year to remarkably precise breeding and wintering locations.
They navigate landscapes and respond to winds, weather, food and environmental conditions across enormous geographic scales.

We see these species and their migrations as among evolution’s great living masterpieces. That’s why we combined science with natural history and artist John Anderton’s extraordinary illustrations of the birds themselves. The maps allow us to see where birds travel, and the art brings the species to life.
Together, they make visible something that humans could only imagine for most of our history.
North America has lost about 3 billion birds during the past half-century, and many migratory species continue to decline.

To understand why a population is declining and help save it, researchers need to understand the species’ entire annual cycle: its critical stopover habitats, wintering grounds and threats along its migration routes.

For much of the history of ornithology, scientists studied birds primarily during their breeding season. That made practical sense. Birds are conspicuous then – singing, defending territories, building nests and raising young.

But a migratory bird may spend only a few months of its life in its breeding grounds. Conditions such as weather, food availability and habitat quality encountered during migration can determine whether an individual survives to breed again.

Drought thousands of miles away can affect a bird’s condition months later. American redstarts depart later after dry winters and produce fewer young. Declining horseshoe crab populations in Delaware Bay have reduced food availability for migrating red knots, contributing to lower survival.
All of this knowledge has accumulated because people value birds and have devoted enormous time and effort to understanding them.

For more than a century, thousands of bird-banders have woken up before the crack of dawn to set traps, carefully place bands on birds’ legs and release them, often knowing the chances of ever learning what happened to those individuals were exceedingly small.

More recently, tracking technology has allowed researchers to follow individual birds across continents and oceans. Those tracks exist because scientists, students, technicians and others have spent countless hours attaching and recovering tags, and contributing and sharing their data.
Today, millions of bird-watchers contribute observations that, thanks to advances in data science, allow us to watch migration unfold across an entire continent.
We have spent much of our careers documenting the decline of birds, and we know the challenges facing migratory species are formidable. But we also have hope for these creatures’ survival.

Scientists today know more about where migratory birds go, how populations are connected and what they encounter along the way than at any previous point in history. That knowledge is helping to identify where conservation efforts can make a difference for the future.

articles.title: Japan’s MMX mission aims to swipe soil samples from Mars’ moon Phobos
articles.author: Daniel Brown, Lecturer in Astronomy, Nottingham Trent University
paras: A Japanese space mission is about to launch towards Mars. But it will not land on the planet itself. Instead, the Martian Moons Exploration (MMX) mission will focus on Phobos, the bigger of Mars’s two small moons.
The mission will lift off on Monday October 19 at 20:41 BST on an H3 rocket from the Tanegashima Space Center, in the south of Japan.

This will start a five-year mission, during which the spacecraft will orbit and explore Phobos, deploy a lander, touch down and collect soil and small pebbles. In a world first, these samples will be delivered to Earth for study in laboratories.

MMX is led by the Japanese Aerospace Exploration Agency (Jaxa), in collaboration with the US, France, Germany and the European Space Agency (Esa). The overall science objective is to unravel the origins of the two Martian moons, the smaller of which is called Deimos. Mission scientists also want to examine the wider evolution of Mars and its local environment in space.
We still have no clear understanding of how the red planet got its moons. These natural satellites could have been hapless asteroids that were passing by Mars when they got captured by its gravity.

Another possibility is that that they formed when an asteroid collided with Mars, causing rocky material to be thrown out into space. Gradually, this material coalesced into Phobos and Deimos. The MMX mission will give us Phobos’s chemical composition, which could help distinguish between theories.

Grabbing samples from Phobos will be no easy task, however. Russia tried this in 2011 with its Phobos Grunt mission. The spacecraft launched successfully to low Earth orbit, but failed to fire its engines to send it toward Mars.

However, Jaxa is well placed to succeed. The space agency has already proved that it can return samples from asteroids with its Hayabusa space missions, which lasted from 2003-10 (Hayabusa) and 2018-20 (Hayabusa 2).

MMX will trial sophisticated sampling techniques designed for Phobos’s low gravity. The moon has about 0.1% the gravitational pull that Earth does. This means that a human on Phobos could jump a distance of 1.5 km horizontally without much effort.

The mission will also be a test of communication between the spacecraft and a newly developed ground station. After launch and deployment, MMX will take a year to reach Mars, arriving in August 2027. It will first circle the red planet before slipping into orbit around Phobos about a month later.

The spacecraft consists of three modules with distinct functions: a propulsion module to get MMX into orbit around Mars, an exploration module with landing and sample collection gear and a return module to deliver the sample to Earth.

The mission will make use of 13 science instruments to explore Phobos. High resolution cameras called Tengoo and Orochi will map the surface and a laser altimeter (Lidar) will build up a picture of the moon’s contours. Lidar uses laser pulses to measure the distance from the spacecraft to features on the surface.

An infrared spectrograph called MIRS will survey Phobos’s minerals, while a gamma ray and neutron detector, called Megane, will determine the moon’s elemental composition. From a greater distance, MMX will also gather data on Mars’s smaller moon Deimos.
The instruments will send back data that controllers will use to decide where and how to land the spacecraft on Phobos.

In early 2029, the MMX exploration module will deploy a small microwave oven-sized rover called Idefix, which has been developed jointly by Jaxa, the French space agency Cnes and the German Aerospace Center (DLR). Idefix will drop down onto Phobos’ surface from between 40 and 100m in altitude.

The rover will then right itself and travel over the surface during an operational period expected to last about 100 days. It will be using several sensors, including a Raman spectrometer and radiometer, to make a final call about where the exploration module should land.

In 2030, the module will swoop down and land on Phobos, remaining on its surface for about 2.5 hours. It will be able to extract samples from the surface once or possibly twice by landing again at a different location. The ability to sample from more than one place on Phobos is vital to understanding the moon’s composition.

The exploration module will use either an instrument called the C-sampler to drill a core or a device knowns as the P-sampler, which blows a jet of nitrogen gas to blast soil and loose pebbles off the surface and into a sample collection chamber.

The C-sampler would be able to collect a core from up to 2cm below the surface. This would provide the mission with a sample composition unaltered by solar radiation, which causes chemical changes to planetary surfaces over time. The P-sampler is a back-up option, but carries some small risk of toppling the spacecraft in low gravitational fields like the one on Phobos.

Having gathered at least 10 grams of material, the spacecraft will leave the Martian moon, separating from its landing gear. It will then travel back to Earth, arriving in 2031. On its approach, the spacecraft will eject its sample probe, which will then descend through Earth’s atmosphere. It will land using parachutes in Australia, where it will be recovered and transported to Japan.

A potential side-benefit of the mission is that samples from Phobos might also include material from Mars. Phobos closely orbits the red planet and is thought to be constantly hoovering up Martian soil. This soil is thought to be regularly ejected from the planet’s surface by asteroid impacts.

MMX could therefore be considered a lite-version of the Mars Sample Return (MSR) mission. MSR, a collaboration between the US and European space agencies, would have sent rock samples from the Martian surface to Earth. However, budgetary pressures led to the programme being effectively cancelled by US Congress.
If scientists get lucky with the samples from MMX, they might get a nice consolation prize.
